usage_notes.narrative: Harris assigns the dominant 7th chord to the major 6 diminished scale family. Every dom7 chord belongs to a family of four related dominants sharing the same diminished triad, built a major 3rd above the dominant note. 'The rule of thumb for finding a related diminished chord is to build it a major 3rd above the dominant note.' Chapter 1, p. 27.

The four dominant 7th chords derived from the same diminished triad are interchangeable when resolving V7-I. Harris illustrates with D7-Gmaj7: F7, Ab7, and B7 are also related to F# diminished and make interesting voicings when played against D in the bass. Chapter 4, p. 83.

When substituting related dominants over a V7-I resolution, Harris prescribes keeping the original dominant root in the bass while shifting the upper voicing to the related dominant chord. The D7-Gmaj7 example shows F7, Ab7, and B7 played against D in the bass, preserving bass-line identity while varying harmonic color. Chapter 4, p. 83.

For the dominant 7th scale, Harris specifies exactly three important arpeggios: on the tonic, the 5th, and the 7th. These are the only arpeggio positions the student prioritizes in practice. Chapter 1, p. 13.

The dominant 7th scale has its own set of scale-degree-specific rules for inserting chromatic half-steps in descending phrases to generate bebop vocabulary. Half-steps typify the language of the bebop player and are an endless source of improvisational ideas. Chapter 1, p. 17.

When applying diminished extensions over dominant 7th chords in minor keys, Harris specifies the diminished chord by key: C7 in F minor uses E-diminished; G7 in C minor uses B-diminished. The related diminished selection is both key- and chord-specific. Chapter 5, p. 93.

Harris assigns the major 6th chord as the primary identity of the major 6 diminished scale family. It is the foundational chord from which all major-function voicings derive via 'a scale for chording, and a method of assigning virtually any chord to one of two scales—the major 6 diminished and the minor 6 diminished.' Chapter 3, p. 66.

The C6 diminished scale—built on the major 6th chord—contains three interlocking diminished chords providing its internal architecture: the C and A belong to one diminished, the E and G to a second, and the B diminished chord provides the other four notes. All voicings within a major-function passage are drawn from this scale. Chapter 3, p. 67.

When moving between major-6-scale voicings, Harris's governing rule applies directly: remember to move each note to the next note of the scale. Each voice in a maj6-family voicing steps to its adjacent neighbor in the major 6 diminished scale, creating smooth voice motion. Chapter 3, p. 71.

Harris collapses the min7 chord into the major 6 diminished scale family by redefining it as an inversion: 'Every minor 7 chord is an inversion of a major 6th chord.' The student should think of any m7 chord not as its own category but as a major 6th chord viewed from a different inversion, unlocking all major-6-diminished voicings for min7 contexts. Chapter 3, p. 69.

Because every min7 chord is an inversion of a major 6th chord, all voicings for a min7 chord are drawn from the major 6 diminished scale of the corresponding major 6th chord. The student assigns the min7 to that scale and applies the standard movable-chord voice-leading rules. Chapter 3, p. 69-71.

Harris names a special role for the min7 chord: 'Important minor is the term given to the chord found on the 5th degree of a dominant 7th scale (5 of 5).' This specific min7—the minor 7th a 5th above the dominant—serves as a reusable harmonic tool in progressions like Rhythm Changes. Chapter 2, p. 46.

Harris collapses the min7b5 (half-diminished) chord into the minor 6 diminished scale family: 'every minor7 flat5 chord is an inversion of a minor 6th chord.' The student should think of any m7b5 as a minor 6th chord in inversion, unlocking all minor-6-diminished voicings for half-diminished contexts. Chapter 3, p. 69.

Because every m7b5 chord is an inversion of a minor 6th chord, all voicings are drawn from the minor 6 diminished scale of the corresponding minor 6th chord. The movable-chord rule applies: move each note to the next note of the minor 6 diminished scale. Chapter 3, p. 69-71.
The minor 6th chord is the foundational identity of the minor 6 diminished scale family, the second of Harris's two universal chording scales. Chapter 3, p. 66.

The minor 6 diminished scale is constructed by fusing the minor 6 chord with its related diminished chord: 'This scale is formed by combining a minor 6 chord with its related diminished chord. The diminished chord is built from a major 3rd above the dominant note of the scale.' Chapter 2, p. 58.

Harris prescribes a specific named voice-leading unit ending on a minor-with-6th-in-bass chord: 'the progression from major to minor to minor with the 6th degree in the bass: (Bb major-G minor-Gm/E).' The min6 position is the cadential arrival of this three-chord formula. Chapter 4, p. 79.

Harris prescribes building the related diminished chord a major 3rd above the dominant note to locate the four interchangeable dominant 7th chords in any key. 'Just go up a major 3rd from the root of the dominant 7th chord.' Chapter 1, p. 27; Chapter 2, p. 42.

Each diminished chord generates exactly four related dominant 7th chords, all interchangeable in cadential contexts. F# diminished generates D7, F7, Ab7, B7. The diminished chord is the organizational hub for a family of four V7 colors. Chapter 4, p. 83.
Within the C6 diminished scale, three interlocking diminished chords provide the scale's internal architecture and serve as symmetric stepping-stones for moving voicings. Chapter 3, p. 67.

In minor key contexts, Harris specifies which diminished chord to apply over each dominant by key: C7 in F minor uses E-diminished; G7 in C minor uses B-diminished. The student selects the related diminished by key signature. Chapter 5, p. 93.

Harris defines the augmented arpeggio as a variant of the major arpeggio with the 5th raised a half-step: 'An Ab augmented arpeggio (the 5th degree is raised a half-step from the major).' It appears in the vocalist's warm-up series as a technical skill prerequisite for improvisation freedom. Chapter 5, p. 95.
